articles.body: Services Top Right Tailwind adds London Thamesport to Dolphin Express service November 26, 2026 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Tailwind Shipping Lines will add London Thamesport to its weekly Dolphin Express (DEX) service at the end of November, establishing new short-sea connections between the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and the Iberian Peninsula. London Thamesport will become the first southbound call after Moerdijk. The revised rotation will be: Moerdijk – London Thamesport – Antwerp – Setúbal – Cádiz – Barcelona – Cádiz – Moerdijk After its second Cádiz call, the service will sail directly to Moerdijk. A feeder connection between Setúbal and Casablanca will continue to extend the DEX network into North Africa. According to Tailwind, the new rotation will offer an eight-day transit from Cádiz to the United Kingdom, while cargo moving from Moerdijk will reach London Thamesport in one day. Tailwind operates the weekly service with Panda 003 , Panda 004 and Panda 005 . The carrier said each vessel has a capacity of 1,380 TEU. articles.title: MPC Container Ships reports lower Q3 earnings amid fleet renewal
articles.summary: MPC Container Ships (MPCC) reported lower revenue and earnings for the third quarter of 2026, while highlighting firm charter demand, extensive forward coverage and continued progress with its fleet renewal programme. Operating revenue declined to US$113.1 million from US$125.9 million in the same period last year,...
articles.body: MPC Container Ships (MPCC) reported lower revenue and earnings for the third quarter of 2026, while highlighting firm charter demand, extensive forward coverage and continued progress with its fleet renewal programme. Operating revenue declined to US$113.1 million from US$125.9 million in the same period last year, while EBITDA fell from US$83.5 million to US$69.9 million. Adjusted for non-recurring items, EBITDA reached US$60.8 million, compared with US$74.9 million in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted profit decreased to US$36.1 million from US$45 million. Fleet utilisation remained high at 97.8%, slightly above the 97.6% recorded a year earlier. MPCC achieved an adjusted average time charter equivalent rate of US$25,333 per day, compared with US$26,523 per day in the corresponding quarter of 2025. Charter backlog supports forward visibility MPCC ended the quarter with a charter backlog of US$2.2 billion. Its fleet is fully contracted for the remainder of 2026, while coverage stands at 90% for 2027, 66% for 2028 and 42% for 2029. “Container demand has held up better than many expected this year, and charter rates reached a four-year high in the quarter,” said Constantin Baack, CEO of MPC Container Ships. “That momentum is carrying into 2027: the fourth quarter has been very strong so far, our charter customers are looking for ships, and forward vessel availability is at its lowest level since 2005,” he added. The company declared a recurring quarterly dividend of US$0.04 per share and reaffirmed its full-year guidance of US$460 million to US$470 million in revenue and US$280 million to US$300 million in EBITDA. Fleet renewal continues During the quarter, MPCC took delivery of the methanol dual-fuel newbuilding DP World Southampton and handed over the 2007-built AS Angelina to its new owners. The company also agreed to sell the 2008-built AS Sicilia , subject to a successful handover. At the end of September, the group’s fleet comprised 64 vessels with an aggregate capacity of approximately 183,800 TEU, including 16 newbuildings on order. Five modern vessels are scheduled to join the fleet by early 2027. MPCC completed an oversubscribed private placement in July, raising gross proceeds of approximately US$108 million. The company ended the quarter with 28 debt-free vessels and a leverage ratio of 26.7%. “Firm asset values and continued strong charter markets allowed us to continue renewing the fleet in the quarter,” said Moritz Fuhrmann, Co-CEO and CFO of MPC Container Ships. “The proceeds from the private placement in July have strengthened our balance sheet, and with moderate leverage and 28 debt-free vessels, we have the financial flexibility to keep investing in the fleet, act on opportunities that arise and continue returning capital to shareholders,” he concluded.

articles.title: KLN Logistics and Hai Robotics expand smart warehousing partnership
articles.summary: KLN Logistics Group has entered into a strategic partnership with Hai Robotics to expand the use of automated warehouse systems across its international logistics operations. Announced on 25 November, the agreement builds on three projects the companies have already completed in Shenzhen and Jiaxing, China, and the...
articles.body: KLN Logistics Group has entered into a strategic partnership with Hai Robotics to expand the use of automated warehouse systems across its international logistics operations. Announced on 25 November, the agreement builds on three projects the companies have already completed in Shenzhen and Jiaxing, China, and the Middle East. The installations serve three international footwear brands and provide a foundation for introducing similar automation solutions to customers in other industries. The partnership combines KLN’s logistics network and warehouse management experience with Hai Robotics’ automated case-handling technology. KLN will identify facilities where robotic systems could improve storage, order processing and operational flexibility, while the two companies work together on solutions tailored to individual customer requirements. Building on existing warehouse automation projects Hai Robotics specialises in Automated Case-handling Mobile Robot (ACR) systems, which are designed to automate the storage and retrieval of goods in warehouses. Through the expanded partnership, KLN plans to make greater use of these technologies across its logistics centre network, drawing on experience gained from the three existing installations. “Technology creates tangible value when applied to real-world operations. Our successful collaboration with Hai Robotics has demonstrated what we can achieve by combining complementary strengths,” said Alan Cheung, Managing Director – China and North Asia at KLN. Cheung said the companies would continue supporting customers through system design, implementation and ongoing improvements, with the aim of strengthening warehouse efficiency and supply chain performance. For Hai Robotics, the agreement offers an opportunity to introduce its automation technology to a broader range of international customers through KLN’s established logistics network. “Our collaboration with KLN has shown the value of combining our intelligent systems with KLN’s global network and logistics expertise,” said Alan Liu, VP, President of Greater China & Japan Regions at Hai Robotics. The partners intend to expand their collaboration beyond the footwear industry, although they have not identified additional customer projects or announced a timetable for further installations. Financial terms, the number of robots deployed and performance figures for the existing projects were not disclosed.

articles.title: ETS for maritime revision – The EU must not miss the opportunity to protect its ports and maritime connectivity
articles.summary: Ahead of the European Parliament’s Environment Committee vote on the maritime EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), FEPORT, representing European private port companies and terminal operators, the European Transport Workers’ Federation (ETF), the European Shippers’ Council (ESC), CLECAT, representing freight forwarders...
articles.body: ETS for maritime revision – The EU must not miss the opportunity to protect its ports and maritime connectivity in Port News 26/11/2026 Ahead of the European Parliament’s Environment Committee vote on the maritime EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), FEPORT, representing European private port companies and terminal operators, the European Transport Workers’ Federation (ETF), the European Shippers’ Council (ESC), CLECAT, representing freight forwarders and logistics providers, the European Community Association of Ship Brokers and Agents (ECASBA), the European Maritime Pilots’ Association (EMPA) and the European Tugowners’ Association (ETA) call on Parliament and Council to act. We cannot miss this opportunity to prevent transhipment traffic from shifting outside the EU and to protect fair competition and connectivity across European ports. The maritime EU ETS applies directly to shipping companies, but decisions about where ships call affect the entire port community. Ports and terminals, dockworkers, ship agents, freight forwarders and other logistics providers, tug and pilotage services, and road, rail and inland waterway operators all depend on regular calls. For cargo owners and European businesses, greater reliance on transhipment through non-EU ports could mean longer lead times, less reliable services and more complex supply chains. We welcome the attention EU institutions are giving to the risk of ETS evasion. The amendment adopted on November 23rd by the TRAN Committee which is now before ENVI combines a voyage-distance criterion with fixed ETS reductions for different categories of port call. Shipping lines support the distance-based approach. For EU ports, however, the approach risks undermining the level playing field. Competing ports can serve the same markets and hinterlands, yet the services calling at them could face different ETS costs because of the length of the voyage. This could make longer routes more attractive and raise the relative cost of services connecting the EU with nearby trading partners. The fixed reductions add a further distortion. Unloading just a few more transhipment containers at a single call could move a vessel into a category with substantially lower ETS costs. That gives shipping lines an incentive to consolidate traffic in fewer ports. Gateway and mixed ports, where transhipment is an important part of a wider business serving EU imports and exports, could lose regular calls. A less diverse port network would weaken maritime connectivity, reduce demand for port and hinterland services and leave shippers and freight forwarders with fewer routing options when disruptions occur. Parliament and Council should give these risks further consideration as the revision progresses. ETS relief should be proportionate to the actual share of containers unloaded at an EU port for onward shipment to a non-EU port. This would target the cargo most exposed to relocation and avoid sharp changes in ETS costs at fixed cargo thresholds. Co-legislators should also consider applying the same principle to the subsequent outbound leg and covering container ships from 5,000 TEU, since some EU transhipment ports mainly serve vessels below 10,000 TEU. Existing customs information should be used wherever possible to limit additional reporting. This approach should be accompanied by stronger criteria for identifying neighbouring container transhipment ports under the ETS Directive and by monitoring how the measure affects the distribution of traffic and services across EU ports. This is the moment to get it right. Parliament and Council should use the remaining stages of the revision to agree a measure that curbs evasion, preserves the environmental integrity of the ETS and protects the port services, jobs and maritime connections that European supply chains depend on. articles.body: Ship Recycling Showing Signs of Weakness in India, Stronger Elsewhere in Hellenic Shipping News 26/11/2026 T he ship recycling market has shown mixed signs across the major markets, during the course of the past week. In its latest weekly report, Best Oasis ( www.best-oasis.com ), a leading cash buyer of ships said that “the Indian ship recycling market has weakened this week, primarily influenced by currency fluctuations, resulting in softer buying indications across vessel categories. Local steel demand remains subdued, with limited buying activity and relatively slow movement in the domestic market. The coming months are traditionally a stronger period for steel demand, raising expectations of improved market activity and renewed buying interest. Overall, market sentiment remains cautious in the near term, although a seasonal recovery in demand could support greater activity in the coming weeks”. Source: Best Oasis Meanwhile, “the Bangladeshi ship recycling market remains firm, with buyers continuing to demonstrate strong interest in acquiring suitable recycling tonnage. Local market conditions have shown some improvement, providing additional support to prevailing buying indications. Overall, market sentiment remains positive, supported by sustained buying interest and relatively stable pricing. The Pakistani ship recycling market remains relatively quiet, with no significant changes in overall market activity. Buying indications have softened slightly compared with the previous week, although buyers continue to express interest in acquiring suitable recycling candidates. Overall, market sentiment remains cautious, with limited activity and softer price indications. The Turkish ship recycling market remains largely unchanged this week, with no significant developments in local market conditions. Buying indications remain broadly stable, with limited movement in overall recycling activity”, Best Oasis concluded. Source: Intermodal Shipbroker In a separate weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal added that “last week, Bangladesh stood out as the strongest of the recycling destinations across the Subcontinent, while Pakistan and India stayed cautious and Turkey remained subdued. In Alang, sentiment weakened as breakers held a cautious stance. Local steel market remained sluggish, with prices slipping from previous levels. Local currency strengthened against the USD, but the recent sharp currency swings add uncertainty. Limited vessels circulated the market, with buyers’ interest more focused on specialist tonnage, rather than the conventional units. Chattogram was firm, with positive sentiment and a strong appetite in acquisitions. Local steel prices rose, although local demand has yet to recover. Taka held unchanged against the US dollar. A few dry bulk candidates were circulated to the market, including a vessel proposed for delivery after about 130 days. Domestic conditions, however, remain fragile: Political tensions, arson incidents and heightened security risks have added uncertainty. Gadani remained quiet, with the market still being cautious. Local steel demand stayed slow; however, scarcity on materials during the week pushed prices higher. Local currency edged slightly firmer against the USD. Few candidates were circulated to the market amid low appetite for further tonnage. On the economic front, a proposed increase in electricity tariffs could put further cost pressure on recyclers. Aliaga was stable. Local steel prices increased on expectations of higher energy costs, while the Izmir steel mill remains shut after last week’s fatal accident. The lira weakened further, hitting a new year-to-date low against the USD. Transactional activity was limited”. articles.title: WSC report highlights global renewable marine fuel opportunities as dual-fuel fleet set to meet 20% of liner energy demand by 2030
articles.summary: Investment in new container ships and vehicle carriers is creating a substantial potential market for renewable marine fuels, according to a new report released today by the World Shipping Council. By around 2030, ships already operating or on order that are capable of using renewable marine fuels are expected to...
articles.body: WSC report highlights global renewable marine fuel opportunities as dual-fuel fleet set to meet 20% of liner energy demand by 2030 in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 26/11/2026 I nvestment in new container ships and vehicle carriers is creating a substantial potential market for renewable marine fuels, according to a new report released today by the World Shipping Council. By around 2030, ships already operating or on order that are capable of using renewable marine fuels are expected to account for more than one-fifth of liner shipping’s total energy demand, demonstrating the scale of potential demand for renewable fuels. However, investment in ships alone will not deliver the energy transition. Without binding global regulations that close the price gap between conventional and renewable fuels, the demand these ships represent risks going unrealised, holding back investment in renewable fuel production and supply infrastructure. Released ahead of the UN’s World Sustainable Transport Day on 26 November, the report highlights opportunities for renewable fuel production and bunkering across Africa, Asia and Oceania, Central and South America, Europe, the UK and Türkiye, and North America. It finds that renewable marine fuels, including both bio-based and synthetic e-fuels, are already being produced and bunkered, although currently on a limited scale. Established fuel industries, renewable electricity resources and existing infrastructure offer opportunities to expand production in both established bunkering markets and new locations. Some existing renewable fuel producers have already indicated they could increase supply in response to stronger demand, highlighting the opportunity to connect growing investment in ships with new production and supply. “Shipping companies are investing in ships capable of using renewable fuels, and this report shows the opportunities for fuel producers around the world to supply them,” said Joe Kramek, President and CEO of World Shipping Council. “The fuels and technologies are already there, but creating a market at scale requires the right commercial conditions. Global regulations that close the price gap with conventional fuels are necessary to unlock investment in production and turn the potential of these ships into real emissions reductions,” Joe Kramek said. The report comes ahead of the International Maritime Organization’s Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting (MEPC 85), taking place from 30 November to 3 December, where governments will meet to discuss global GHG regulations for shipping. WSC is calling for binding global measures with a credible pathway to net zero, consistent enforcement across all ships and incentives to help close the price gap between conventional and zero- and near-zero GHG fuels. articles.title: New clause available for tanker ship-to-ship transfers and special operations
articles.summary: We have published a new standard clause for ship-to-ship transfers and other transfer operations involving tankers and gas tankers. The BIMCO Tanker Ship-to-Ship Transfer and Special Operations Clause 2026 provides a contractual framework for allocating the operational responsibilities, costs and risks associated...
articles.body: New clause available for tanker ship-to-ship transfers and special operations in International Shipping News 26/11/2026 W e have published a new standard clause for ship-to-ship transfers and other transfer operations involving tankers and gas tankers. The BIMCO Tanker Ship-to-Ship Transfer and Special Operations Clause 2026 provides a contractual framework for allocating the operational responsibilities, costs and risks associated with these increasingly important operations. The new clause covers cargo operations carried out by ship-to-ship (STS) transfer as well as transfers to or from inshore and offshore installations. It was originally developed as part of our work on CO2TIME 2026, where the drafting subcommittee considered the operational requirements associated with the carriage of liquefied CO₂. During that work, it became clear that the issues addressed by the provision were relevant beyond the emerging CO₂ trade. Vessels capable of carrying liquefied CO₂ may also carry other cargoes, while STS transfers and transfers involving offshore installations are already an important feature of tanker and gas tanker operations. We have decided to publish the clause as a standalone clause that can be incorporated into tanker and gas tanker charter parties. Clear allocation of responsibility The clause gives charterers the right to order the vessel to conduct STS transfers or transfers to and from inshore and offshore installations. As these operations arise from the charterers’ employment of the vessel, the associated risk, cost, expense and time are placed with the charterers. At the same time, the clause contains important operational safeguards. Charterers are responsible for providing adequate equipment, including fendering and hoses, and operations must comply with the latest relevant guidance issued by organisations such as OCIMF, INTERTANKO, ICS and SIGTTO, or other applicable international standards. Importantly, the master’s authority over the safety of the vessel is preserved. Transfer operations are subject to the master’s approval and discretion, and the master may suspend or discontinue an operation if it is, or may become, unsafe. Where the master considers additional expertise necessary, the clause also allows for an experienced mooring master or superintendent to be employed by the owners at the charterers’ cost. The parties involved in an STS operation must agree in advance who will have overall charge of the transfer, without affecting the master’s ultimate discretion in relation to the safety of the vessel. Insurance and regulatory requirements The clause also addresses some of the additional financial and regulatory consequences that can arise from STS and other special transfer operations. Where an operation requires an extension of the owners’ or vessel’s existing insurance cover, or results in other additional costs or expenses, the charterers are responsible for the additional premium or expense, subject to their prior approval and the owners providing supporting documentation. Responsibility for obtaining the necessary permissions from relevant authorities also rests with the charterers, together with the associated costs. Owners may request documentary evidence that the necessary authorisations have been obtained and may verify the position directly with the relevant authorities. By bringing these elements together in a single provision, the BIMCO Tanker Ship-to-Ship Transfer and Special Operations Clause 2026 provides parties with a clear contractual solution for operations that can involve additional operational complexity, regulatory requirements and risk. The clause is intended for incorporation into tanker and gas tanker charter parties where STS transfers and transfers involving inshore or offshore installations may form part of the vessel’s employment. articles.title: STEALTHGAS INC. Reports Strong Third Quarter Profits
articles.summary: STEALTHGAS INC., a ship-owning company serving the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sector of the international shipping industry, announced its unaudited financial and operating results for the third quarter and nine months ended September 30, 2026. articles.body: STEALTHGAS INC. Reports Strong Third Quarter Profits in Hellenic Shipping News 26/11/2026 STEALTHGAS INC., a ship-owning company serving the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) sector of the international shipping industry, announced its unaudited financial and operating results for the third quarter and nine months ended September 30, 2026. OPERATIONAL AND FINANCIAL HIGHLIGHTS Strong profitability continued for the third quarter, with Net income of $24.5 million corresponding to a basic EPS of $0.65, 41.6% higher than the previous quarter’s $17.3 million and 83.9% higher compared to the $13.3 million achieved in the third quarter of 2025. Revenues recorded were $40.2 million in the third quarter, same as the previous quarter and 9.6% lower compared to last year’s third quarter. TCE rates improved for the larger vessels but were slightly reduced for the smaller vessels due to idle time, representing an average daily TCE of $13,886. Continued focus on period coverage. About 60% of fleet days for 2027 are secured on period charters, with total fleet employment days for all periods generating about $115 million (excl. our single JV vessel) in contracted revenues. All of the vessels in the fleet are unencumbered. The Company has paid down all its bank debt since Q3 2025. The Company strengthened its liquidity with cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments of $269.2 million as of September 30, 2026 and over $275 million currently. Third Quarter 2026 Results1: Revenues for the three months ended September 30, 2026, amounted to $40.2 million compared to revenues of $44.5 million for the three months ended September 30, 2025, based on an average of 25.0 vessels and 29.0 vessels owned by the Company, respectively. The decrease in revenue is primarily attributable to the decreased average number of vessels in our fleet. Voyage expenses and vessels’ operating expenses for the three months ended September 30, 2026, were $9.4 million and $12.3 million, respectively, compared to $7.2 million and $15.0 million, respectively, for the three months ended September 30, 2025. The $2.2 million increase in voyage expenses was mainly due to an increase in bunker costs driven by higher bunker prices and an increase in war risk insurance expenses. The $2.7 million decrease in vessels’ operating expenses was mainly due to the decrease in the average number of vessels. Drydocking costs were $0.7 million for each of the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025 . General and administrative expenses for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, were $3.6 million and $1.9 million, respectively. Depreciation for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, was $5.7 million and $6.6 million, respectively. The $0.9 million decrease is mainly related to the decrease in the average number of vessels owned by the Company. Other operating gain for the three months ended September 30, 2026, was $12.4 million compared to nil for the same period last year, resulting from the insurance claim settlement relating to vessel Eco Wizard. Gain on sale of vessels for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was $0.2 million compared to nil for the same period last year. The gain was attributable to the sale of two vessels during the three months ended September 30, 2026. Interest and finance costs for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, were $0.001 million and $0.2 million, respectively. The $0.2 million decrease from the same period of last year is primarily due to full debt prepayments. Equity earnings in joint ventures for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, were gains of $1.6 million and $1.1 million, respectively. The $0.5 million increase is primarily due to the higher charter rates of the JV vessel. As a result of the above, for the three months ended September 30, 2026, the Company reported net income of $24.5 million, compared to net income of $13.3 million for the three months ended September 30, 2025. The weighted average number of shares outstanding, basic, for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025 was 36.9 million and 36.0 million, respectively. Earnings per share, basic, for the three months ended September 30, 2026, amounted to $0.65 compared to earnings per share, basic, of $0.36 for the same period of last year. Adjusted net income was $13.0 million corresponding to an Adjusted EPS of $0.35 for the three months ended September 30, 2026 compared to Adjusted net income of $14.4 million corresponding to an Adjusted EPS of $0.39 for the same period of last year. EBITDA for the three months ended September 30, 2026, amounted to $27.5 million. Reconciliations of Adjusted Net Income, EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA to Net Income are set forth below. An average of 25.0 vessels were owned by the Company during the three months ended September 30, 2026 compared to 29.0 vessels for the same period of 2025. Nine months 2026 Results: Revenues for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, amounted to $126.0 million compared to revenues of $133.8 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2025, based on an average of 26.4 vessels and 28.4 vessels owned by the Company, respectively. The decrease in revenue is primarily attributable to the decreased average number of vessels in our fleet. Voyage expenses and vessels’ operating expenses for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, were $22.8 million and $38.9 million, respectively, compared to $16.7 million and $41.2 million, respectively, for the nine months ended September 30, 2025. The $6.1 million increase in voyage expenses was mainly due to an increase in bunker costs driven by higher bunker prices and an increase in war risk insurance expenses. The $2.3 million decrease in vessels’ operating expenses was mainly due to the decrease in the average number of vessels. Drydocking costs for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, were $3.7 million and $1.8 million, respectively. Drydocking expenses during the nine months of 2026 mainly relate to the completion of four vessels’ drydockings, compared to the same period of last year which included the completion of two vessel’s drydockings. General and administrative expenses for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, were $7.5 million and $6.1 million, respectively. articles.title: Global patchwork of shipping decarbonization rules looms after COP31 collapse, warns PortXchange
articles.summary: Maritime emissions tracking and reducing specialist PortXchange has warned that shipping is heading for a costly patchwork of national and regional climate rules unless International Maritime Organization (IMO) member states adopt the Net-Zero Framework next week, after the UN climate summit in Antalya collapsed...
articles.body: Global patchwork of shipping decarbonization rules looms after COP31 collapse, warns PortXchange in Port News 26/11/2026 Maritime emissions tracking and reducing specialist PortXchange has warned that shipping is heading for a costly patchwork of national and regional climate rules unless International Maritime Organization (IMO) member states adopt the Net-Zero Framework next week, after the UN climate summit in Antalya collapsed without a deal. COP31 closed on 22 November without a final text, the first time since 2009 the annual summit has failed to agree, after Saudi Arabia and other oil producers forced fossil fuel language out of the draft. Eight days later, IMO member states meet for MEPC 85 (30 November to 3 December), with the resumed extraordinary session on 4 December expected to decide the framework’s fate. The last attempt, in October 2025, was postponed by 57 votes to 49 after the United States threatened tariffs, visa restrictions and port fees against countries backing the framework. “COP and the IMO are watching the same film,” said Sjoerd de Jager, Managing Director and Co-Founder of PortXchange. “A handful of countries whose economies run on oil and gas are blocking what most of the world has already said it wants. At COP they deleted the words. At the IMO, they went further and threatened the trade of anyone who voted the other way.” The delay is already costing the transition. The UCL Energy Institute and Getting to Zero Coalition’s Climate action in shipping 2026 report calls last year’s failure to adopt the framework “the single most transition-regressive event” in its five years of tracking. The share of tonnage on order that can run on scalable zero-emission fuels fell from 9.5% to 5.7%, while conventional-only ships rose from 54% to 61% of the orderbook. Even if it is adopted next week, the framework cannot take effect before 2029. The Global Maritime Forum counts 84 active green shipping corridors worldwide, yet only four have reached the stage where vessels, infrastructure or fuel plants are actually being built or operated. The cost gap between conventional and low-carbon fuels is the main brake. Sjoerd De Jager – Managing Director of PortXchange “Nobody on the water is short of ambition. Owners are electrifying barges, trailing hydrogen-derived fuels and asking the IMO, again and again, for clear rules,” said de Jager. “What kills most corridors between pilot and operation is the operating cost: someone has to pay the premium on green fuel and electricity. The Net-Zero Framework is the only measure on the table built to close that gap worldwide and a few governments are holding it back while the rest of the industry pays for it.” Without a global deal, countries and regions will keep writing their own rules. The EU already applies its ETS and FuelEU Maritime to ships, and the Netherlands and Spain have added national obligations on marine fuel suppliers. Since July, the UK has run a separate carbon price, the UK ETS, on domestic voyages and on emissions while ships of 5,000 GT and above are in UK ports. Every extra layer adds compliance work for operators trading across borders and pushes cost and cargo from one market to the next. The UK Chamber of Shipping has asked for any extension of the UK ETS to international voyages to wait until the IMO completes its Net-Zero Framework negotiations, so the December 4 decision will also shape how far that patchwork spreads in UK waters. “If member states walk away again on 4 December, the IMO’s authority as shipping’s global regulator takes a hit it may not recover from,” said de Jager. “What replaces it is a patchwork of regional carbon prices and fuel rules and ships cross every border, so this industry will pay for that fragmentation more than any other.” PortXchange is urging ports and operators to act whatever the vote. Synchronizing arrivals so ships slow down at sea instead of waiting at anchor cuts fuel burn straight away. At the Port of Algeciras, real-time port call coordination through PortXchange’s Synchronizer cut idle time per vessel arrival and departure by nearly 40% and avoided an average of 32.9 tonnes of CO2 per port call. Measuring emissions call by call with EmissionInsider then shows where shore power and other investments will make the biggest difference. “Member states have one job on 4 December: adopt the framework as it stands,” de Jager said. “Another year of delay is a decision too and the industry will remember who took it.” He also set a challenge for the industry itself: “Stop waiting for London. Every port and every operator can cut emissions this year with data and tools that already exist. If governments won’t lead, the industry has to and the companies that move now will be ready for whatever rules finally arrive.” Source: PortXchange 2026-11-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: EU decision to target biocides in antifoulings raises industry concerns
articles.summary: The recent vote by EU Member States in favour of the European Commission’s proposal not to renew the approval of Selektope®, a non-lethal biocide, signals the EUs intention to ban the use of all biocides used in antifoulings protecting vessels in European waters. In the last decade, rising fuel costs and increasingly...
articles.body: EU decision to target biocides in antifoulings raises industry concerns in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 26/11/2026 The recent vote by EU Member States in favour of the European Commission’s proposal not to renew the approval of Selektope®, a non-lethal biocide, signals the EUs intention to ban the use of all biocides used in antifoulings protecting vessels in European waters. In the last decade, rising fuel costs and increasingly strict regulations on emissions and the spread of alien invasive species have put shipping under growing pressure to improve their environmental performance. According to Markus Jönsson (CEO I-Tech), owners have responded by investing in increasingly sophisticated biocidal antifouling technologies to maintain clean hulls. “Biocides are a critical component of modern antifouling coatings, helping the shipping industry lower fuel consumption and corresponding emissions while also helping to prevent the spread of invasive aquatic species,” he says. “We believe that this decision risks putting European shipyards and the wider maritime industry at a competitive disadvantage, limiting the technologies they can offer while driving future antifouling innovation outside the EU.” Markus Jönsson, CEO I-Tech; Photo courtesy of I-Tech Jönsson cites a 2021 study commissioned by the International Maritime Organisation that found that even a light layer of small calcareous growth on an average container ship can increase greenhouse gas emissions and fuel consumption by up to 55 per cent. “We believe the EU’s decision to start blocking the renewal of biocides in the EU is not consistent with the industry’s environmental goals,” he says. “And with other biocidal suppliers facing EU scrutiny in the coming months and years, there is growing concern that the current Biocidal Product Regulation (BPR) review process could drive these valuable technologies from the market precisely when shipping needs them most.” The EU’s BPR will not only make it more difficult for the industry to meet its decarbonisation targets and protect marine biodiversity, it will also slow innovation, making the European shipping industry less competitive. “By limiting what coating manufacturers and shipyards can develop and offer in Europe, owners may turn to other shipbuilding regions where marine coatings containing advanced biocidal technologies are readily available,” he says. Jönsson also expressed concerns over the methodology behind the BPR ruling, a view shared by more than 50 stakeholders including shipowners, coating manufacturers, active-substance suppliers, trade organisations and antifouling experts who were invited to comment during the public consultation period. “Stakeholders challenged the EU’s assessment of some of the biocidal alternatives, pointing out that few options offer comparable protection against hard fouling. Drawing on practical experience, they argued that the non-biocidal technologies identified by the EU cannot replace existing solutions across all vessel types and operating profiles,” he says. “Proactive and reactive hull cleaning can help manage fouling, but both have particular limitations against hard fouling and are no substitute for biocides.” Others have noted that the BPR review process works against the EU’s own decarbonisation agenda and pending legislation on invasive species. They also see it as at odds with the EU’s Maritime Industrial Strategy, released in March 2026 to boost competitiveness and technological leadership. “This lack of regulatory consistency sends a confusing message to the industry at a time when global warming is accelerating and marine biodiversity is in decline,” says Jönsson. “Under the BPR, the EU should look beyond hazard classifications before ruling out a technology. It should compare where alternatives can be used, how well they work in service and what risks they pose to people and the environment. The comparison should also cover their wider environmental impacts over the full life cycle and what switching would mean for the industry and society.” Jönsson acknowledges that because the EU’s non-renewal decision for medetomidine, the active ingredient in Selektope®, only applies to vessels constructed for trade in EU waters only, it will have minimal commercial consequences for shipowners and for I-Tech. In fact, Selektope®remains available globally and to approximately 95 per cent of the registered fleet. But by removing technology from Europe’s antifouling toolbox, he worries that it will have a negative impact on European innovation and competitiveness. ”We hope the EU will reconsider the impact of their approach to biocides in antifoulings as they move forward,” says Jönsson. “The EU decision is unfortunate but does not alter I-Tech’s commitment to supporting customers, coating manufacturers and shipowners worldwide.” Source: I-Tech 2026-11-26 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: In the last decade, rising fuel costs and increasingly strict regulations on emissions and the spread of alien invasive species have put shipping under growing pressure to improve their environmental performance.
According to Markus Jönsson (CEO I-Tech), owners have responded by investing in increasingly sophisticated biocidal antifouling technologies to maintain clean hulls.
“We believe the EU’s decision to start blocking the renewal of biocides in the EU is not consistent with the industry’s environmental goals,” he says.

The vessel was launched on 17 August and is owned by Fukuyoshi Kaiun. It was constructed by Koike Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering as the third vessel in the Maya class, following the delivery of the first ship in 2024. Representatives from the Kobe City Port and Harbor Bureau and Hanshin Port presented commemorative gifts to Captain Tadahiro Yabuta. Minato measures 96.81 metres in length and 14 metres in width. It has a gross tonnage of 749 tonnes and a deadweight of 1,711 tonnes. The vessel is powered by a 2,600 PS Hanshin Diesel Works LA34G main engine. Imoto Lines said the new vessel will support the expansion of maritime container transport through the modal shift of international feeder and domestic cargo. The carrier aims to contribute to lower energy consumption, reduced logistics costs and greater route diversification within Japan’s distribution network.

articles.title: APM Terminals and Port of Rotterdam prepare terminal expansion
articles.summary: APM Terminals Maasvlakte II and the Port of Rotterdam Authority are preparing a new phase of expansion at the Maasvlakte II container terminal. It will add 25 hectares of terminal area, about 711 metres of additional quay and supporting port infrastructure, and is expected to raise annual capacity by roughly 1.4...
articles.body: APM Terminals Maasvlakte II and the Port of Rotterdam Authority are preparing a new phase of expansion at the Maasvlakte II container terminal. It will add 25 hectares of terminal area, about 711 metres of additional quay and supporting port infrastructure, and is expected to raise annual capacity by roughly 1.4 million TEU once complete. The terminal has been investing in its facilities at Prinses Amaliahaven since 2008, and the expansion is being delivered in phases while the existing terminal stays fully operational. The first part has recently come into service. The two organisations will divide the work. APM Terminals Maasvlakte II will concentrate on developing terminal operations, while the Port of Rotterdam Authority, in cooperation with the terminal, will prepare the site for construction and deliver the maritime infrastructure. That includes extending the existing quay wall by 711 metres and the landside crane rail by 428 metres, and dredging about 1.3 million cubic metres of sand. The new infrastructure will add capacity for deepsea, feeder and inland shipping vessels. The terminal is fully automated, with electrified equipment, automated guided vehicles and remotely operated quay cranes. Harold Kunst, Managing Director of APM Terminals Maasvlakte II, called the expansion the next step in the terminal’s long-term development, creating space for future growth while continuing to serve customers safely, reliably and efficiently, and said the collaboration with the Port Authority is essential. Boudewijn Siemons, CEO of the Port of Rotterdam Authority, said the investment in additional capacity and modern infrastructure strengthens Rotterdam’s position as Europe’s leading container port, increases the resilience of logistics chains, contributes to security of supply and supports the competitiveness of the Dutch economy.

articles.title: Freire Shipyard Celebrates Launch of New Greenpeace Vessel
articles.summary: Freire Shipyard celebrated the launch ceremony of NB 737 on November 25, 2026 in Vigo, marking a milestone in the construction of Greenpeace International's new flagship vessel. Designed to support environmental campaigns and scientific research worldwide while minimizing fossil fuel consumption…
articles.body: Freire Shipyard Celebrates Launch of New Greenpeace Vessel Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 25, 2026 © Greenpeace International Freire Shipyard celebrated the launch ceremony of NB 737 on November 25, 2026 in Vigo, marking a milestone in the construction of Greenpeace International's new flagship vessel. Designed to support environmental campaigns and scientific research worldwide while minimizing fossil fuel consumption, the vessel is scheduled for delivery by the end of 2027. With an overall length of 75 meters, the new sailing vessel has been designed to undertake demanding, long-range maritime operations, including campaigns in polar regions. Its design prioritizes energy efficiency, combining wind propulsion with an intelligent energy generation, storage and management system to minimize fossil fuel consumption. The vessel will feature a range of energy generation and storage technologies, including solar panels, battery storage systems, energy recovery systems and hydrogen fuel cells. These will be complemented by four dual-fuel internal combustion engine generator sets for electricity generation designed to use green methanol (MeOH) as their primary fuel, with small quantities of marine gas oil (MGO) used to initiate combustion. One of the key features of the design is the automated DynaRig sailing propulsion system, comprising two rotating masts with a combined sail area of 1,746 square meters. Under favorable weather conditions, this configuration will enable the vessel to circumnavigate the globe using wind power alone. In addition, while sailing, the propellers will be able to operate as generators, harnessing the vessel's movement to produce electricity. The aim is for the vessel to operate with minimal fossil fuel use from the outset, with a view to eliminating it entirely as the necessary supply chains and infrastructure become available. In addition, the vessel will feature onboard laboratories, systems for deploying remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), a helideck equipped to support helicopter operations, and four auxiliary boats that can be deployed even in challenging sea conditions. With the addition of NB 737, Greenpeace will expand its fleet, which currently comprises the Rainbow Warrior Ill, the Arctic Sunrise and the Witness, further strengthening its capacity to carry out environmental campaigns and scientific research in defense of the environment.

articles.body: Paolo Piacenza, President of the Southern Tyrrhenian and Ionian Sea Port Authority, has signed the decree awarding the demolition of the former Civam industrial building and the construction of a new commercial logistics area beside the Bengasi dock in the port of Vibo Valentia Marina. The project has a total value of EUR 1.5 million. Following a competitive tender, the contract went to La Martina Appalti Srls of Villa Literno, in the province of Caserta, for EUR 863,887. Work is due to start within days and will last 180 days from delivery of the site. The works involve complete demolition of the old industrial warehouse and the subsequent construction of new yards to support port handling and logistics activities. This reclaims a space now occupied by a defunct structure and returns it to a use consistent with the port’s operational needs. Its strategic position near the Bengasi dock will improve the organisation of port spaces, make commercial activities more efficient and strengthen the port’s ability to meet the needs of operators and the local production system. The project belongs to the 2026-2028 Three-Year Operational Plan and to a wider development strategy for the port, which includes investments to upgrade infrastructure, improve the efficiency of port spaces, raise security and strengthen links between the port, economic activities and the surrounding area. The transformation aims to make Vibo Valentia Marina more functional, competitive and integrated with the local manufacturing sector by reclaiming existing areas and creating spaces suited to the new needs of commercial ports. Piacenza described the redevelopment as a concrete step in the modernisation and revitalisation of the port, saying the area can be fully restored to its former port function and used for strategic commercial logistics services. He said the goal is to make the port more efficient and better equipped, supporting local economic activity and creating new development opportunities.

BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI/Pool via REUTERS/File Photo By Alicia Diaz (Bloomberg) –The US announced plans to impose a fresh round of tariffs on goods from China, the European Union and a dozen other economies under President Donald Trump’s push to restore sweeping global import taxes that the Supreme Court found unconstitutional. The rate for imports from China would rise to 20%, in line with the country’s prior agreement with the Trump administration — though that rate could double to 40% if talks between the two countries fall apart, according to a senior US official. The official briefed reporters on condition of anonymity ahead of Wednesday’s announcement. Products from the EU will be taxed at 15% in compliance with the US’s deal with the bloc, though that could also rise to as much as 20%, according to the Office of the US Trade Representative. Tariffs will apply to items from economies the Trump administration accuses of overproduction in some domestic industries and hurting American companies. They are still subject to a public comment process and could change. A final action could come as early as January, the official said. The new levies mark the latest effort by the administration to reinstate an expansive tariff agenda that included country-by-country levies implemented using emergency powers. Those were struck down by high-court justices in February, forcing Trump to invoke other legal authorities to advance his agenda. It’s a politically risky move. Democrats swept to a landslide victory in the midterm elections earlier this month thanks in part to voter anger over the cost of living and disapproval of the president’s handling of the economy. China and the EU could also retaliate, though initial signals from them were muted. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a briefing earlier Wednesday that the prospect of new US tariffs on its exports was “political maneuvering” and said the two nations should work together to maintain their trade truce. The announcement appears to comply with the 2025 trade agreement between the US and EU, which capped tariffs at 15% on most of the bloc’s exports. As a result, the move likely won’t antagonize transatlantic relations for now. European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said “we strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity” and added the bloc expects new levies to abide by the tariff agreement. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new duties were designed to preserve existing deals while addressing overcapacity concerns. “A lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it,” Greer said Wednesday on CNBC. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we’re proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in.” Imports from Japan, South Korea, Switzerland — all prominent US trading partners — would be hit with a 15% rate. The number could go up to 25% for Korea and 20% for the other two, USTR said. Indian products would face a 17% charge if a trade pact with Washington is finalized, though that could increase to 25%. Several smaller nations in Asia were also hit. Similar expected measures aimed at Mexico and Norway were not included but remain under consideration, the official said. Greer said on CNBC the US has “had some very good conversations with Mexico” on the issue. The tariffs follow a probe that began in March into alleged excess manufacturing capacity, utilizing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a process seen as more resistant to legal challenges than Trump’s prior tariff wall. The tariff rates aren’t expected to surpass already agreed-upon levels in trade agreements with each economy. The move will test the tolerance of economic partners, who have largely held back from retaliating, opting instead to negotiate deals with the US to minimize their tariffs. That dynamic could be on display next month, when Trump meets again with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of the Group of 20 summit. Their trade truce is set to expire in January unless the two powers agree to extend it. “If we were to go beyond the 20% or something like that, they would view that as breaking our deal,” Greer said, The trade ambassador said Washington and Beijing are also “proposing to implement” tariff reductions under its new board of trade on around $30 billion of non-sensitive exports. Greer signaled that the new levy will not stack on top of existing duties of 10% or 12.5% under a separate investigation into negligent enforcement of forced-labor laws. “Those are not really additive,” he said on CNBC. For products eligible to be hit by both sets of duties, only the higher rate would apply, the official said earlier. The official added that there would be goods exempted from the tariffs, including oil and gas and food products that cannot be grown in the US. Other products that are already subject to sectoral duties, including tariffs on pharmaceuticals and critical minerals, are also exempted. After the Supreme Court loss, Trump immediately announced plans to rebuild his tariff wall under a different legal authority. Under the Section 301 framework, the president can implement tariffs following an investigation into allegedly unfair foreign trading practices. While Section 301 tariffs are seen as more legally sound and flexible than other powers Trump has eyed, they’re also more time-consuming. An earlier investigation under the same legal authority into policies around forced labor from US trading partners resulted in tariffs on some 60 economies. Those duties are currently facing legal challenges. The new tariffs apply to Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, and Vietnam. USTR also announced it is raising tariffs on imports from Brazil, altering a previously-conducted trade investigation into the country’s digital policies and trade practices. The US is considering increasing the out-of-quota tariff rate on raw and refined sugar and proposing a 10% tariff on finished aircraft. The increased levy on imports from Brazil comes weeks after Trump ally Flavio Bolsonaro lost his presidential election bid to progressive incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy IMO The International Maritime Organization (IMO) is calling on shipping companies to make more training berths available to cadets, highlighting a longstanding disconnect between the industry’s need for qualified seafarers and the lack of opportunities for young people to gain the sea time required to enter the profession. In many developing countries, aspiring officers complete their shore-based maritime education only to spend years waiting for an onboard training placement, even as shipping companies struggle to recruit qualified personnel. In an announcement Tuesday, the IMO outlined efforts to expand its NextWave Seafarers initiative, which aims to address the bottleneck through cooperation between governments, shipowners and maritime training institutions. More than 80 participants representing over 25 countries gathered at IMO headquarters in London on November 20 to formally launch the second phase of the initiative and explore ways to increase the availability of onboard training opportunities. The program’s pilot phase, developed in partnership with Saudi Arabia’s Transport General Authority and national shipping company Bahri, saw 19 cadets from developing island nations and least developed countries complete their onboard training aboard Bahri vessels. The second phase aims to train at least 30 additional cadets, with women accounting for half of participants. The IMO also wants to recruit at least five shipping companies to provide training berths, laying the groundwork for a wider international partnership. The workshop examined practical barriers to cadet placements, including visa restrictions complicating crew changes, as well as the importance of providing a safe and supportive working environment for young seafarers entering the industry. The shortage of training berths exposes a fundamental challenge in addressing the industry’s workforce needs. Expanding maritime education alone will do little to increase the supply of qualified officers if graduates cannot secure the mandatory sea time needed to earn their professional credentials. Without sufficient participation from shipowners, the industry risks leaving a pool of prospective seafarers untapped at a time when it needs to attract and retain the next generation of maritime professionals. The IMO is encouraging shipping companies and governments interested in supporting the initiative, including by offering training berths, to contact its Technical Cooperation and Implementation Division at [email protected] . articles.title: Red Sea and Indian Ocean Nations Advance Plans for Combined Maritime Security Force
articles.summary: Countries bordering the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean are moving toward establishing a combined maritime task force to combat piracy, strengthen regional security and protect commercial shipping across some...

Photo courtesy EUNAVFOR Countries bordering the Red Sea and Western Indian Ocean are moving toward establishing a combined maritime task force to combat piracy, strengthen regional security and protect commercial shipping across some of the world’s most strategically important waterways. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) announced that signatories to the Djibouti Code of Conduct and its Jeddah Amendment have adopted a new Regional Maritime Security Strategy and agreed to advance plans for a Combined Maritime Task Force (CMTF). The agreement was reached during a high-level meeting held November 11–13 in Antananarivo, Madagascar. The proposed task force would build on existing national and regional maritime security capabilities, improving coordination among participating countries. Governments agreed to develop the force’s legal framework and concept of operations in 2027. The initiative comes amid persistent threats to commercial shipping in the Red Sea and renewed concerns over piracy off the Horn of Africa, underscoring the need for greater regional cooperation in protecting international trade and seafarers. The broader security strategy covers the Western Indian Ocean, Gulf of Aden and Red Sea. Preparatory work began in Saudi Arabia in November 2024, with government representatives, navies, coast guards and maritime law enforcement agencies subsequently meeting in Mombasa, Kenya, earlier this month to finalize the framework. Originally adopted in 2009 in response to Somali piracy, the Djibouti Code of Conduct was expanded in 2017 through the Jeddah Amendment to address a wider range of maritime security threats. Somalia’s Minister of State Mohamed Abdulkadir Mohamed emphasized the human cost of attacks on commercial shipping during the meeting. “The protection of seafarers is not simply a maritime security obligation; it is a fundamental humanitarian responsibility,” he said. The meeting also marked a leadership milestone, with Tanzania’s Stella Katondo becoming the first woman elected to chair the regional initiative. South Africa will serve as deputy chair. While the agreement represents a significant step toward a more coordinated regional security presence, the proposed task force remains in development. The IMO has not announced a deployment timeline or details of participating naval assets. articles.title: PIL and Qingdao Port complete China’s first bio-LNG bunkering for international shipping
articles.summary: Pacific International Lines (PIL) and Qingdao Port have completed what they describe as China’s first liquefied bio-methane (LBM) bunkering operation for an internationally trading vessel. The operation took place at Qingdao Port’s QQCTN terminal, where PIL’s LNG dual-fuel containership Kota Odyssey received...
articles.body: Pacific International Lines (PIL) and Qingdao Port have completed what they describe as China’s first liquefied bio-methane (LBM) bunkering operation for an internationally trading vessel. The operation took place at Qingdao Port’s QQCTN terminal, where PIL’s LNG dual-fuel containership Kota Odyssey received ISCC-certified LBM through a truck-to-ship transfer. It also marks the Singapore-based carrier’s first use of the renewable fuel in its fleet. Produced from organic feedstocks, LBM, also known as bio-LNG, can be used in LNG dual-fuel engines without modifying the vessels’ existing machinery. PIL is introducing the fuel as part of its efforts to reduce shipping emissions while expanding its fleet of dual-fuel containerships. According to the carrier, the batch supplied at Qingdao is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by more than 70% compared with conventional fuel oil, based on a well-to-wake lifecycle assessment. PIL also estimates a reduction of around 70% compared with fossil LNG. PIL advances alternative fuel adoption The bunkering operation represents a further step in PIL’s fleet decarbonisation programme, which combines new vessel investments with energy-efficiency technologies and the gradual introduction of lower-emission fuels. Since 2022, the company has ordered 28 LNG dual-fuel containerships, providing greater flexibility to adopt renewable alternatives as commercial supplies increase. “This milestone demonstrates the flexibility PIL has built into our fleet renewal programme,” said Abhishek Chawla, Chief Marine Officer, PIL. The vessel involved, Kota Odyssey, was delivered to PIL in 2024 and operates on the carrier’s SWS service connecting Asia and West Africa. For Qingdao Port, the operation demonstrates its ability to supply renewable LNG alternatives to international shipping companies. The port is working to expand its alternative fuel services as demand for lower-emission marine fuels develops. “This maiden biomethane bunkering service is a major milestone for China’s green shipping transition,” said Yijie Zhang, Head of the Energy Business Department, Ark Intelligence, Qingdao Port. Zhang added that the partnership with PIL supports Qingdao’s development as a regional green bunkering hub. The companies did not disclose the volume of LBM supplied during the operation or the commercial terms of the bunkering arrangement.

Finnish Border Guard/Handout via REUTERS ROME, Nov 25 (Reuters) – Italy has told Ukraine it was wrong to attack Russian ships in Libyan waters and warned Kyiv not to spread the war to new areas, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani told Corriere della Sera newspaper on Wednesday. “It was a mistake to violate Libya’s sovereignty,” Tajani said, adding that Rome had received no advance warning of the Ukrainian operations. “Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv’s intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port,” said the minister, who is head of the coalition Forza Italia party. Ukraine has said the maritime drone attack against a Russian naval corvette and a cargo ship at the weekend was a legitimate act of self-defence. Tajani said he had telephoned his Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, to express his concerns, stressing Italy’s commitment to Libya’s territorial integrity. Another coalition party, the far-right League, also condemned the attack, calling it “unacceptable” and warning that it risked destabilising the north African country. Italy has been a staunch supporter of Ukraine since Russia’s 2022 invasion, providing military aid and backing European sanctions against Moscow. However, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government has sent mixed signals, with her own party firmly behind Kyiv while the League, led by Matteo Salvini, has repeatedly criticised continued military assistance to Ukraine. Tajani said that Rome would carry on supporting Kyiv’s sovereignty while seeking to prevent the conflict from spreading. “Italy will remain on Ukraine’s side. Ours is a strategic choice,” he said. articles.summary: A record 2,100-plus migrants arrived in Spain's Canary Islands over 24 hours in overcrowded boats, maritime rescue service data showed on Wednesday, prompting regional leader Fernando Clavijo to call for a European-level response to the crisis."The Canaries can't take it anymore.
articles.body: Canary Islands Receive Recording-Breaking Number of Migrants In Single Day Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 25, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Halina A record 2,100-plus migrants arrived in Spain's Canary Islands over 24 hours in overcrowded boats, maritime rescue service data showed on Wednesday, prompting regional leader Fernando Clavijo to call for a European-level response to the crisis. "The Canaries can't take it anymore. We're experiencing an unprecedented migration pressure," Clavijo wrote on X, adding that he had requested an urgent meeting with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. "These people come to Europe and it's not fair that we alone respond to a drama of this magnitude," he said. One migrant was found dead in a boat and another gave birth during the perilous crossing from West Africa, the rescue service said. The daily arrivals surpassed the previous record of about 1,500 set two weeks ago. Most of the boats arrived at El Hierro, an island of some 11,400 residents that has become one of Europe's key entry points for migrants from West Africa. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who has faced tough criticism of his open stance on migration during the campaign ahead of Sunday's parliamentary election, said on Wednesday Europe needed a comprehensive approach to migration, including stronger border controls in cooperation with Senegalese and Gambian authorities. Still, he said Spain needed "to open legal migration pathways" for workers in sectors such as housing that are short of qualified labour. The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is one of the world's deadliest migration crossings as migrants seek to reach Spanish territory despite rough seas, strong currents and long distances. Arrivals tend to pick up in the autumn months, when sea conditions along the route are generally calmer and more favourable for crossings. Arrivals so far this year had climbed to 28,103 as of late November, more than last year's total but still well below an all-time high of 46,843 recorded in 2024, when most crossings occurred during the first nine months of the year. Nearly 21,000 people have reached the archipelago in the last two months. (Reuters)

articles.body: Εverllence and China COSCO SHIPPING Corporation Limited have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to develop digital services for the shipping group’s fleets. The agreement was signed on 23 November 2026 and expands their existing cooperation from individual COSCO SHIPPING companies to the group level. The aim is to develop digital solutions that can be used across different fleets, helping improve vessel operations, maintenance and fuel efficiency. Digital services to support fleet operations Under the agreement, Everllence and COSCO SHIPPING will explore common digital requirements across the group’s shipping businesses. This approach could allow new services to be developed centrally and then adapted to the needs of individual fleets. One of the first areas of cooperation may involve the digital delivery of main-engine specifications and selected 3D equipment models. The work would follow relevant China Classification Society guidelines. COSCO SHIPPING Vice President Luo Bing said the group aims to strengthen cooperation in data standards, green ship technologies and smart shipping applications. Julian Seemüller, Head of Digital Asia Pacific at Everllence, said the agreement would help the company develop solutions based on the operational requirements of a major global shipowner. “The group-level framework gives us a clearer view of which digital services can be applied across different fleets and where they need to be adapted to specific requirements,” said Seemüller. Partnership builds on previous engine cooperation The agreement builds on the companies’ existing relationship in marine propulsion and technical services. In October 2025, Everllence announced the methanol dual-fuel conversion of a B&W S90 two-stroke engine aboard the COSCO SHIPPING Libra containership. The project was carried out by Everllence’s PrimeServ division in cooperation with COSCO SHIPPING Heavy Industry. The latest MoU extends that relationship into digital fleet services. According to Everllence, combining engine data with technical expertise could help shipowners improve equipment availability, reduce fuel consumption and manage maintenance more efficiently. The companies have not disclosed the financial terms of the agreement or announced a timetable for deploying the proposed digital services.

articles.title: Houston Ship Channel trade grows
articles.summary: Trade activity across the Houston Ship Channel region continued to grow, reinforcing the waterway’s role in supporting American industry, jobs and economic activity. articles.body: Trade activity across the Houston Ship Channel region continued to grow, reinforcing the waterway’s role in supporting American industry, jobs and economic activity. Foreign tonnage rose 15% year to date through September to 200.2 million tons, driven by a 20% rise in exports, and deep draft vessel transits increased 12% in October. The region remains central to US energy exports. Through September, Houston accounted for 32% of US crude oil exports and nearly 65% of the year-to-date increase in national oil exports, with the Netherlands, Mexico and Japan its three leading destinations. Domestic cargo is also significant: based on US Army Corps of Engineers indicators and historical data, Port Houston estimates that 67.6 million short tons moved through the region in the first nine months of 2026, up about 3.8% from an estimated 65.1 million short tons a year earlier. At Port Houston’s public terminals, October container volume reached 415,326 TEUs, up 14 percent year on year and the highest October on record. Loaded imports hit an all-time monthly high of 199,302 TEUs, surpassing the previous record set in May, and loaded exports climbed to an October record of 144,334 TEUs. Through the first ten months of 2026 the port handled a record 3.76 million TEUs, up 4%. Growth extended beyond containers: steel tonnage at the public terminals increased 74% to 504,010 tons, and general cargo rose 170% to 217,633 tons, with steel, packaged cement and other industrial materials supporting construction, manufacturing and energy-related industries. Charlie Jenkins, CEO of Port Houston, described the Houston Ship Channel as an economic engine for the region, supporting jobs and businesses across Texas and the nation, with the industries along it moving the goods and materials that keep the economy running.

articles.body: NYK Line, Partners to Advance Remote Ship Emissions Monitoring Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 25, 2026 Conceptual image of the system (Credit: NYK Line) Shipping company NYK Line and seven other organizations have signed an agreement to develop remote sensing technology capable of measuring greenhouse gas emissions from vessels without physical contact, with trials focused on Yokohama Port in Japan. The agreement, signed on November 25, brings together NYK Line, MUFG Bank, Nagoya Electric Works, ArkEdge Space, Shimizu Corporation, the City of Yokohama, Yokohama-Kawasaki International Port Corporation and Yokohama Port Corporation. The collaboration will advance the True Emission Eye - Maritime project, which aims to develop technology for measuring, visualizing and quantifying greenhouse gas emissions from ships at a distance. The project will conduct measurements on actual vessels at Yokohama Port to assess the technology's accuracy, while examining system specifications, potential applications and opportunities for future commercial deployment. The technology is being developed to complement existing methods of estimating vessel emissions based on fuel type and consumption, providing a means of directly measuring emissions from outside ships. The system uses optical observation technology that exploits the ability of gases, including carbon dioxide, to absorb and emit light at specific wavelengths. Data obtained from vessel exhaust observations is combined with physical parameters, including distance to the ship and weather conditions, to calculate emissions. Testing has already been conducted at experimental facilities and on NYK Group vessels, both at berth and underway. At Yokohama Port, the project has captured infrared images of ship exhaust from observation points including Osanbashi Pier and the Yokohama Bay Bridge Skywalk. The images are being compared and analyzed against vessel data to evaluate the technology. The partners will continue conducting measurements under different conditions to improve the accuracy of the system, while also examining fixed-point monitoring at ports. The project will also assess the technical requirements for satellite-based observations of ship emissions and explore the potential integration of satellite measurements with ground-based data. The eight organizations aim to bring the technology into practical use to improve transparency in vessel emissions reporting and support decarbonization across the shipping and port sectors.

articles.body: Dutch Shipowner Picks Wärtsilä Engines for Four Newbuilds Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 25, 2026 (Credit: Royal Wagenborg) Wärtsilä has secured an order to supply engines for four new 14,000-deadweight-tonne general cargo vessels being built for Dutch shipowner Royal Wagenborg, extending its involvement in the company's EasyMax 2.0 fleet renewal programme. The four vessels will be equipped with Wärtsilä 25 engines, following the selection of the same engine type for the first two EasyMax 2.0 ships in 2025, the Finnish technology group announced on November 25. The new vessels are being constructed at Royal Niestern Sander shipyard in the Netherlands, with deliveries of Wärtsilä equipment scheduled to begin in 2027. The engine order was booked in the fourth quarter of 2026, although its financial value was not disclosed. The Wärtsilä 25 features a modular architecture designed to enable future conversion to alternative low- and zero-carbon fuels as they become commercially available. Each engine will also be equipped with Wärtsilä's NOx Reducer (NOR) emissions after-treatment system, which uses selective catalytic reduction technology to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions. The engine selection forms part of Wagenborg's EasyMax 2.0 design, which focuses on fuel efficiency, operational flexibility and reduced emissions. Wagenborg operates a fleet of more than 160 vessels, with Wärtsilä equipment installed on over half of them. The companies also maintain a long-term service agreement covering engines and propulsion systems across Wagenborg's fleet. The latest order follows the use of Wärtsilä 32 engines on the shipowner's previous EasyMax vessels.

articles.title: Most Large Fuel Tankers Now Ship ‘Dirty’ Crude, Upending Trading
articles.summary: A record three-quarters of the global fleet of large tankers designed to transport oil products are tapping higher earnings to ship crude, keeping the cost to move fuels elevated.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Avigator Thailand/Shutterstock By Weilun Soon Nov 25, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A record three-quarters of the global fleet of large tankers designed to transport oil products are tapping higher earnings to ship crude, keeping the cost to move fuels elevated. Less than a quarter of the world’s 542 long-range 2, or LR2, tankers are currently transporting “clean” cargoes such as jet fuel, naphtha and diesel as of this week, according to Signal Ocean data. The vessels have cargo holds that are coated to transport refined fuels, and have to undergo an expensive cleaning process to return to the trade once they ship “dirty” crude oil. The shift in use of the LR2 fleet comes as crude flows recover through the Strait of Hormuz. A system of shuttling tankers and ship-to-ship transfers has helped exports from the Persian Gulf recover to pre-war levels, boosting freight rates and prompting charterers to tap smaller vessels to meet demand. Benchmark earnings for very-large crude carriers have soared, in turn enabling smaller-sized tankers — including Aframaxes, which are the crude-focused equivalent of LR2s, able to hold about 750,000 barrels — to command far higher fees. And an LR2 that dirties up can charge Aframax earnings. Shipping executives often look at how many LR2s are switching to plan on how much they can charge, and how they should deploy their tankers around the world. Even though the LR2 fleet has grown 12% since January last year and clean-fuel shipments have fallen due to the US-Iran war, the increased switching to crude has helped put a floor underneath the fees they can command to carry oil products. “Tracking LR2 employment between clean and dirty trades is becoming as important as monitoring the size of the fleet itself,” Signal analysts Maria Bertzeletou and Georgios Sakellariou said. The switching of LR2s started last year as traders sought to store more crude on vessels at sea, but accelerated in the initial phase of the Iran War from the end of February, when refineries in the Middle East were attacked by the Islamic Republic — reducing the need for clean tankers, Sakellariou said. Read More: Oil Tankers Get ‘Dirty’ Ditching Fuels for Crude as Rates Boom A lot of the processing plants in the region remain unavailable, reducing the need for products tankers. About 1.7 million out of the more than 9 million barrels a day of refining capacity is currently offline in the Middle East, RBC Capital Markets analysts including Christopher Louney and Helima Croft wrote in a note this week. Around 1 million barrels a day of that potentially needs months to repair, they said. Charterers are turning to smaller product tankers, with the share of LR2s in transporting fuels falling to just 12% between July and September, from almost 18% a year earlier, Signal data show. Meanwhile, a benchmark freight index reflecting daily LR2 earnings from the Mediterranean to Asia increased more than five-fold, while another from the Middle East to Europe jumped more than 10-fold in the year through end-September. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P.
